content: It is essential to suppress viral load as much as possible to improve overall health outcomes for individuals living with HIV. This indicator can be derived from the HEI register and HIV patient cards of HIV-infected mothers over a specified time period. Given the potentially low number of such cases, it may be necessary to review all patient cards rather than relying on a sample. The proportion of individuals enrolled in HIV care who had their tuberculosis (TB) status assessed and recorded during their last visit is a critical indicator of TB screening coverage in HIV care. The high comorbidity of TB among HIV patients underscores the importance of assessing active TB at every clinical visit. Simplified algorithms that include TB symptoms enable lay health workers to assess and refer patients from the community as needed. If the proportion of patients assessed for TB is low, it is crucial to investigate the underlying reasons. The first step is to determine whether the issue stems from poor data quality. For example, are health workers assessing TB status but leaving the relevant column blank? Alternatively, is it a matter of poor quality of care, where health workers record not done (ND) instead of conducting the assessment? Or is it a combination of poor data quality and care, where TB status is not assessed at all, and the column is left blank? Observing clinical encounters, either by a clinical mentor, supervisor, or trained mystery patient, can help clarify the root cause of the problem. The second step involves addressing the identified issue. If the problem is related to poor data quality, it is necessary to understand why health workers are leaving the column blank. Is it due to inadequate training or a lack of understanding of how to complete the patient card? Are the codes too complex? Do health workers lack sufficient time? If the issue is related to poor quality of care, it is important to determine why health workers are not assessing TB. Are they unfamiliar with the protocol? Do they lack the necessary training? Are they constrained by time? Or do they not perceive TB assessment as a priority? In many cases, both data quality and care quality issues may coexist. At the facility level, this indicator can be derived from a sample of all HIV patient cards over a specified time period. The eligible population includes all patients. This indicator is an additional key metric for monitoring and improving HIV care. The methodology for assessing data quality involves desk reviews, data verification, and system assessments. Another approach is the use of lot quality assurance sampling (LQAS), a method adapted from industry that classifies health centers or other lots as having good or poor data quality based on predetermined thresholds and associated sampling and decision rules. For example, Malawi used LQAS in its national AIDS program to evaluate the accuracy of routine reports by health facilities. Electronic medical record (EMR) systems play a critical role in improving data quality and reducing loss to follow-up in resource-limited settings. These systems should be harmonized and integrated into national health management information systems (HMIS). Standardized data elements and indicators are essential for ensuring consistency and facilitating data exchange. The use of standardized tools also supports supervision, aggregation, and the transfer of patients between facilities. The transition from paper-based to electronic patient monitoring systems requires careful planning and adaptation. Revised paper tools must be printed and distributed, while electronic systems need to be reconfigured with appropriate linkages to the HMIS and other systems. The process of updating an HIV patient monitoring system involves 16 recommended steps, including forming a technical workgroup, engaging stakeholders, inventorying current tools, defining indicators and minimum datasets, and developing training materials. A successful HIV patient monitoring system relies on collaboration among various partners within the health sector, including HIV programs, national programs, and community-based organizations. Integration of HIV data into other program records and the HMIS is critical for ensuring a comprehensive and sustainable approach to patient care. Human resources and capacity-building are fundamental to the success of patient monitoring systems. This includes task-shifting to lower-level cadres and lay providers, as well as providing necessary training, clinical mentoring, and supervision. Staff roles and responsibilities must be clearly defined, and ongoing support should be provided to ensure accurate and efficient implementation of patient monitoring activities. In summary, a robust HIV patient monitoring system is essential for improving the quality of care and health outcomes for individuals living with HIV. It requires a coordinated effort across multiple levels of the health system, with a focus on data quality, integration, and capacity-building.
